title: Why Your AI Committee Keeps Stalling
author: Mike Kentz
summary: Mike Kentz diagnoses why school and campus AI committees repeatedly stall out: institutional discussions conflate two separate questions — the ethical question of whether/when students should use AI, and the pedagogical question of how to build critical student cognition. He describes a familiar, frustrating meeting pattern where curriculum conversations quickly devolve into academic-integrity panic, debates over syllabi language or detection software, and end with no structural progress and an exhausted faculty. Rather than blaming faculty resistance or administrative sluggishness, Kentz argues the real problem is architectural — institutions are structurally set up in a way that guarantees this loop. Building on his earlier piece 'Separate AI Literacy and Assessment Integrity,' he proposes a 'two-charter split' to decouple AI literacy governance from assessment-integrity governance, aiming to resolve the institutional paralysis that keeps stalling policy progress.
points: Identifies a core conflation driving AI-committee paralysis: ethical vs. pedagogical questions get blurred together.
Describes a recognizable meeting pattern: curriculum talk devolves into integrity panic, syllabi/detection-software debates, and stalls out exhausted.
Rejects the common explanation of faculty resistance or administrative sluggishness as the real cause.
Argues the gridlock is an architectural/structural error in how institutions set up AI governance, not a people problem.
Proposes a 'two-charter split' — separating AI literacy from assessment integrity — as the structural fix, building on his earlier essay.
quotes: the tendency to blur the ethical question of whether/when to use AI with the pedagogical question of how to build critical student cognition
If you've sat in a Senate meeting, a working group, or a Dean's council over the last academic year, you've likely felt this paralysis firsthand.

The conversation starts with curriculum design, pivots instantly to academic integrity panics, devolves into a debate over syllabi language or detection software, and ends with little structural progress and an exhausted faculty.
We often attribute this gridlock to faculty resistance or administrative sluggishness. I don't think either are the real issue.
It's more of an architectural error. Most institutions are running.
